analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale, manufacture, and transfer of semiautomatic assault weapons and high-capacity ammunition magazines.
analysis.headline: An assault weapons ban with 84 House sponsors never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess a long list of semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns defined as assault weapons — including AR-15 and AK-style rifles and specific models named in the bill — along with ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds. Guns people already legally owned would be grandfathered, but future sales and manufacturing would stop, and transfers of grandfathered weapons to another person would have to go through a licensed dealer for a background check. The bill also funds voluntary gun buy-back programs and requires date markings on the affected weapons and magazines.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in communities affected by mass shootings and gun crime, who would face a smaller future supply of military-style semiautomatic rifles and high-capacity magazines. Police would also benefit from new reporting on assault weapons used in crimes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess the semiautomatic weapons it defines as assault weapons, cutting off future commercial supply [S2].
It bans large-capacity ammunition feeding devices — magazines that accept more than 10 rounds — except for devices already lawfully owned [S2].
It requires the Attorney General to keep a public record of the make, model, and circumstances of any assault weapon used in a federal or state crime, reported to Congress annually [S2].
It lets local governments use Byrne Justice Assistance Grant funds to pay people who surrender assault weapons or high-capacity magazines under buy-back programs [S2].
Transfers of grandfathered assault weapons between private individuals must go through a licensed dealer and the existing background-check system [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers and dealers who sell the affected rifles, pistols, shotguns, and magazines would lose those product lines, and the market value of newly made banned guns would drop to zero. Owners of grandfathered weapons would face new restrictions on how they can sell or transfer them and new safe-storage duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and current owners

drawbacks.text: The ban turns on features like pistol grips, barrel shrouds, and threaded barrels rather than how fast a gun fires, so critics argued it outlawed guns by appearance while a long list of functionally similar firearms was exempted by name in Appendix A [S3].
Grandfathered weapons stay legal, so the bill would not remove any already-owned gun from circulation, limiting how much it could change the stock of weapons on the street [S2].

Owners of grandfathered weapons would face a new legal duty to store them so that people prohibited from owning guns cannot access them, and could no longer sell or give them away without paying a licensed dealer to run a background check [S2].
The buy-back funding is permissive, letting local governments use existing grant money rather than guaranteeing compensation to owners who surrender weapons [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would steadily shrink the future supply of the specific rifles and high-capacity magazines used in many mass shootings, and it imposes that limit only on future sales while leaving current owners' property untouched. The honest cost side: the feature-based definitions are blunt, exempting thousands of functionally similar hunting and sporting guns by name, and the effect of the earlier 1994 federal ban on overall gun violence was hard to measure, so the public-safety payoff is contested. The burden falls on manufacturers, dealers, and a subset of gun owners rather than on the general public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, and it never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Carolyn McCarthy introduced the Assault Weapons Ban of 2013 in the House on January 29, 2013 [S1].
Eighty-three House members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced [S5].
On February 28, 2013, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations [S5].
No further action was taken for the rest of the 113th Congress; the bill never came out of committee and never received a House vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and dealers of the named AR-15, AK, and similar models kept an open market, and current owners kept full resale rights on their grandfathered weapons, because the ban never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and existing gun owners

for.name: Carolyn McCarthy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Assault Weapons Ban of 2013 in the House.

for.name: 83 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill, letting it sit in a crime subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the 2013 assault weapons ban effort in Congress, including this House bill and its Senate companion.

sides.party_line_note: All 83 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat, with no Republican support recorded; the House's Republican majority controlled the committee calendar.

industries.industry: Semiautomatic rifle manufacturers (AR-15 and AK-style rifles)
industries.note: The bill names these rifles among banned weapons and bans any semiautomatic rifle with a detachable magazine plus features like a pistol grip or threaded barrel, ending legal new production and sales of a fast-growing product line. Their sales depend on continued civilian access that the bill would cut off.

New manufacture, sale, and possession of magazines over 10 rounds would be a federal crime, with seizure and forfeiture provisions, eliminating the high-capacity magazine market. Their revenue runs directly against the bill's public-safety aim.

industries.industry: Traditional hunting and sporting firearms makers
industries.note: Appendix A exempts by name roughly 2,000 bolt-action, lever-action, pump, and other hunting and competition rifles and shotguns, so the bill locks in that segment's market as the unrestricted alternative. Their interest ran alongside the carve-out that keeps their products legal.

Dealers would lose sales of the banned models but gain a guaranteed role: every private transfer of a grandfathered assault weapon must run through a licensed dealer for a background check, for a fee. The lost product line outweighs the new transaction business.
